tracks.title: Three lifetimes, one rule
tracks.text: Lesson 02 point 14 — tokens. This one is under the Nexus, the engine you deploy to your own cloud. So you deployed it… and now two anxieties collide. [curious] One — it's on the public internet, what's the lock? Two — the security reflex everyone's been trained on. Rotate your credentials. Regularly. On a schedule. And here Workbooks does something that looks heretical. It mints the engine's main token once… and then refuses to rotate it. [curious] This lesson is why that's discipline, not negligence. The whole idea fits in one sentence — the lifetime of a token is the blast radius of rotating it. Where rotation is free, it happens constantly. Where rotation is catastrophic, the system makes generation idempotent… so you can't rotate by accident.

tracks.title: Rotate everything, until it breaks you
tracks.text: First — rotate everything, until it breaks you. Here's what rotating a deployed engine's bearer actually does. Every live client holding the old token — your CLI, your CI job, the cron script, the teammate who wired it into their shell — gets a four-oh-one at the same instant. There is no overlap window. [sighs] Rotation isn't hygiene here. It's an outage you scheduled for yourself. The code says so, in a comment, word for word — never rotate on subsequent applies, rotation would four-oh-one all live clients. And rotating the signing key is worse. That one doesn't lock anyone out — it un-signs your history. Every artifact the engine ever produced was attributed to an identity derived from that key. Regenerate it… and every prior signature stops verifying. The chain survives… the attribution dies. Hold onto that asymmetry. It's the most concrete sentence on the page, and we'll earn it.

tracks.title: Three tokens, three lifetimes
tracks.text: So — three tokens, three lifetimes. The Nexus mints three credentials, and they are not the same thing wearing three names. There's a table on the page, but you don't need to see it — let me give you the four rows, and the one column that explains all the others. The last column is — what does rotation break. First… the desktop per-boot token. Minted by the local runtime, every boot. Its lifetime — every boot. What rotation breaks — nothing. The shell just re-reads a file on the same disk. Second… the cloud bearer, WB underscore PUBLIC underscore BEARER. Minted once per deployment. What rotation breaks — every live client holding it, all at once. Third… the signing key, WB underscore SIGNING underscore KEY. Minted once, ever. What rotation breaks — every signature and ledger the engine ever produced. And fourth, the outlier… a J-W-T, the login rung. Rotates constantly, by design. What rotation breaks — nothing. Now hear the symmetry. The first and the fourth rotate maximally… and rotation breaks nothing for either, because neither has to be shipped to clients who'd be caught holding a stale copy. The two in the middle are the dangerous ones — and they're the two the system mints exactly once. [excited] Lifetime tracks blast radius. That's the whole lesson. Everything else is mechanism.

tracks.title: The once machine
tracks.text: The once machine. The cloud bearer is born on your first deploy apply — before the provider recipe ever runs. The function is named ensure cloud bearer, and the word ensure is doing the work. It doesn't generate. It guarantees one exists. Run it a hundred times… and you get exactly one token. Picture the flow as a single fork. The deploy starts, and it asks one question — is WB PUBLIC BEARER already in secrets dot env? If yes… it returns an empty string. Reuse, say nothing, silence. If no… it fills thirty-two bytes from the OS random source, hex-encodes them to sixty-four characters, saves the file, chmods it six-hundred, and prints a one-time notice. Both branches then continue to the deploy. That no branch — the silent reuse — is the heart of the machine. [curious] And the notice itself is the only time you'll ever see this token printed. It tells you to export WB ENGINE TOKEN equals the value… and then it makes a promise, in parentheses — stored in secrets dot env, will not be regenerated on future applies. Run apply a second time and you get… no notice. The same token. Idempotent. You cannot rotate this token by re-deploying, because the most natural thing you'd do — apply again — leaves it untouched.

tracks.title: One env var locks the plane
tracks.text: One env var locks the plane. Persisting the token isn't enough — it gets forwarded into the engine as WB PUBLIC BEARER. And the instant that variable is set and non-empty… the engine's posture changes. There is no separate enable-auth switch. The presence of the variable is the lock. One knob. Inside the engine, every request falls down a five-rung ladder, first match wins. Picture the request dropping through it. Rung one — is the path on the public allowlist? Health, the well-known docs? Then it's open, always. Rung two — is this the desktop app, presenting its per-boot token? Rung three — is the plane locked, and does the bearer match, compared in constant time? Rung four — is there a valid login token, a J-W-T? And rung five, the dev fallback — the x-tenant header — which only fires when the plane is not locked and not multi-tenant. Here's the line that matters most. The moment the lock exists… that dev fallback dies. A locked engine with no bearer presented returns four-oh-one, authentication required, with no fallback at all. Setting the variable didn't add a layer on top of dev mode. It ended dev mode. You can watch it with curl. Hit slash health — you get ok, it's public. Hit the library with no bearer — four-oh-one, authentication required, because it's locked. Hit it with a wrong bearer — four-oh-one, unauthorized, the constant-time compare failed. Hit it with the real token — two hundred, and your tenant is whatever WB TENANT says, defaulting to local.

tracks.title: The client half
tracks.text: [curious] Now the client half. The engine reads the secret as WB PUBLIC BEARER. Clients present the very same secret under a different name — WB ENGINE TOKEN. Same sixty-four hex characters, two roles. One is the lock's combination… the other is you dialing it. Picture the round trip. The client sends a request with no Authorization header — the engine answers four-oh-one. The client attaches Authorization, Bearer, the token — the engine runs the constant-time compare against WB PUBLIC BEARER — and answers two hundred, tenant equals WB TENANT. Same handshake whether you point at a cloud URL or a local engine. And when the token is wrong, the CLI doesn't bury it. It exits with a dedicated auth message that names the two ways out — the engine rejected your credentials, set WB ENGINE TOKEN, or re-run deploy local to refresh discovery. If you got a four-oh-one wiring a script into CI… that's the sentence to read. Either the token's stale, or you're pointed at a cloud engine without exporting it.

tracks.title: Reading the rung first
tracks.text: A depth rung — reading the rung first. There's a chicken-and-egg in that ladder. A client needs to know which credential an engine wants… before it can present one. The allowlist solves it. Three paths are always open, lock or no lock — and one of them is the capabilities doc, at slash well-known slash workbooks-runtime. A client reads it with zero credentials to learn the rung it must satisfy. The doc is plain text. It has an auth field with a rung — trusted, for a shared-bearer engine, or oidc-jwt for one behind an identity provider. It has a tenancy — single. And it has a list of capabilities the engine offers — things like oql, workflow, instances, workbook, agent, library, search, publish. [curious] So a client reads that, and before it risks a single guarded request, it knows — this engine speaks the trusted rung, so I'd better have a bearer ready… and here's exactly what I can ask for once I'm in.

tracks.title: The one that does rotate
tracks.text: Another depth rung — the one that does rotate. This is the contrast that proves the whole thesis. The desktop app's runtime mints a fresh token every single boot. Twenty-four bytes of randomness, base64, held in memory for the life of the process. New every time the app starts. By the hygiene reflex… this is the model citizen. Maximal rotation. But ask why it can rotate so freely. The token is written to a discovery file, on the same local disk the desktop shell reads from. There's no client across a network holding a stale copy. When the token changes… the shell just re-reads the file. [excited] Rotation has no distribution problem here — so it has no rotation problem. The desktop token rotates maximally for the exact reason the cloud bearer can't. Nobody is downstream of it but a sibling process on the same machine. Same idea — a random token a runtime mints — two opposite policies. And the only variable that flipped… is whether anyone has to be told the token changed.

tracks.title: The token that is a name
tracks.text: The token that is a name. The third credential isn't a password at all. WB SIGNING KEY is a thirty-two byte Ed25519 seed — and from it the engine deterministically regrows the same keypair on every redeploy. That keypair is the engine's identity. Its decentralized identifier — the same did-key form Radicle and the W3C spec use. Rotate it… and you haven't changed a lock. You've become a different person. Here's the mechanism. The keystore lives on the container filesystem… which is wiped on every redeploy. Without a persisted seed, each redeploy mints a brand-new keypair — a new identity. And every run the engine ever sealed records the identity it was signed under. Picture the fork at redeploy. The question — is the seed persisted? If yes… the engine regrows the same keypair, the identity is unchanged, and every old ledger still verifies on both counts. If no… it mints a fresh keypair, the identity changes, and now look closely at the old ledgers. They check two separate things. First — tamper evident, is the hash chain intact? That still passes. Nobody touched the data. Second — attributable, does the signature match the recorded identity? That now fails… for every prior ledger. One redeploy, all history orphaned. The chain survives… the attribution dies. That's the asymmetry from the top of the lesson, made literal. So you pin the seed once, before anything signs. Generate thirty-two random bytes, stage it as WB SIGNING KEY, apply — and your identity holds across every redeploy after. One honest caveat — today only the primary tenant's key is seed-pinned. Other tenants regenerate on redeploy, an acknowledged gap. If you're single-tenant, the seed covers you completely.

tracks.title: Rotating anyway
tracks.text: Rotating anyway. Sometimes you genuinely must rotate the bearer — it leaked, someone left, the laptop walked off. There is, very deliberately, no rotate verb. The absence is the design. You do it by hand, in three steps. First — unset the secret, deploy secrets unset WB PUBLIC BEARER. Second — apply, and ensure cloud bearer, seeing no token, mints a fresh one. Third — redistribute the new WB ENGINE TOKEN to every client. And the cost, honestly — every client four-oh-ones until it's updated. No overlap window. The exact timing of when the new secret releases is the provider's, not the kit's… so don't assume it's atomic. Plan the redistribution before you unset. Now the signing key — it has no equivalent path, on purpose. You don't rotate a name. If you regenerate the seed, you haven't refreshed a credential — you've disowned every signature the engine ever made. The right move is to keep it. Persisted, backed up, for the life of the identity.

tracks.title: What this isn't
tracks.text: The honest part — what this isn't. First — the bearer is a shared secret, not an identity. Everyone who presents it is the same tenant. There is no per-user attribution under this rung. If you need to know who did something… that's the login rung, the J-W-T, with a real identity provider behind it. Multi-tenant requires that rung — the shared bearer is a single-tenant lock. Second — the token has no scopes and no expiry. It doesn't time out, it doesn't carry permissions, it can't be narrowed to one capability. It's two hundred fifty-six bits of randomness, compared in constant time, full stop. That's a feature for what it's for — nothing to parse, nothing to expire, nothing to get subtly wrong — and a limit you should know. A leaked bearer is total access until you do the manual rotation. And third — the secrets file is plaintext on disk, protected by six-hundred file permissions and nothing more. No encryption at rest beyond the mode bits. Treat the file as the secret it contains. [curious] None of these are bugs. They're the honest shape of a shared secret — and knowing the shape is how you defend the design in a security review.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Where's my token — I lost the notice? It's in secrets dot env, in the wbx app dir. The list command shows key names only, never values, so you open the file to read it — it's yours, mode six-hundred. The notice is one-time. The file is forever. Do I set the signing key before first apply? Yes. Before anything signs. If the engine signs its first ledger under an auto-generated key and you set the seed later, that early history is orphaned. Is the bearer per-user? No. Everyone presenting it is one shared tenant. Per-user means the login rung. What if the secrets file leaks? Rotate, manually — unset, apply, redistribute. No overlap window, so line up the redistribution first. And — why a hex string, not a J-W-T? [chuckles] Because there's nothing to expire and nothing to parse. A J-W-T carries claims and a signature and an expiry to verify on every request. This token carries none of that — it's a constant-time compare against one variable. The simplicity is the security surface.

tracks.title: Back up to the Nexus
tracks.text: So that's tokens. Three credentials… three deliberately different lifetimes… and one rule underneath all of them — the lifetime of a token is the blast radius of rotating it. The desktop token rotates every boot, because rotation breaks nothing. The cloud bearer is minted once per deployment, because rotation would four-oh-one every client. The signing seed is minted once, ever — because it isn't a credential, it's a name. [curious] The way back up is short. This page is the credential mechanics under one parent — the Nexus, the engine these tokens lock. Go there for the bigger picture of the plane you deployed… and how the secrets stay inside it. Everything here was just the lock on its door.
